children: The Reserve Bank of India’s concessional swap facility has proven to be a blockbuster, garnering $136.38 billion in foreign currency inflows through August 31. While this massive influx successfully achieved its initial goal of stabilising the rupee, it has handed Indian lenders a steep challenge: a "problem of plenty".

Its primary motive of stabilising the rupee against the dollar has been largely achieved. But then there is an opportunity cost for everything in this world. In this case, it is the problem of plenty. The inflow of this money means banks have an additional ₹13 lakh crore to lend. This number is likely to rise from here, as the window for concessional swaps on FCNR-B has ended, but the window for dollar-denominated swaps continues until the end of this calendar year.

This is where basic banking comes into play. The banks garners deposits on which it pays interest. It then deploys these deposits as loans on which it earns interest. The arbitrage between the cost of deposits and the yield on advances is largely a bank’s net interest margin (NIM), which has been on the decline lately.

This sudden wave of liquidity acts as a temporary anchor, keeping a lid on domestic market interest rates and short-term certificate of deposit (CD) spreads despite broader upward rate pressures. However, against a global and domestic macroeconomic backdrop of rising interest rates, banks must navigate a delicate spread environment.

The central bank’s concessional swap framework provides significant operational relief: the RBI bears the entire 3% per annum swap cost on FCNR-B deposits and caps the swap cost at 1.5% for dollar-denominated bonds. This saves banks an estimated 280–300 basis points in currency hedging costs. However, absorbing the hedging cost does not relieve lenders from paying interest on these foreign liabilities.

The margin impact depends on the success of each bank in finding new borrowers. Banks are likely to deploy these funds primarily towards dollar-denominated corporate loans, trade finance, lending through GIFT City and overseas branches, and, to a smaller extent, liquid treasury and interbank assets. “A sizable portion of the mobilised funds is already being routed through international banking units and GIFT City platforms,” says Pandya.

In the short-term, undeployed funds or those lent to low-yielding funds will squeeze margins. Some analysts are still optimistic. “Banks may see some margin pressure, but higher deposit volumes could still make the exercise earnings-positive,” says Maahir Mani of Deven Choksey.
While cheap foreign deposits help contain immediate liability costs, lenders cannot simply dump capital into risky domestic credit expansion just to clear liquidity.

“Just because they’ve got cheap deposits, will the banks become even more aggressive? Perhaps not. Their net interest margins (NIMs) have been under pressure. Till four to five months back, we were worried that certificate of deposit (CD)- overnight index swap (OIS) spreads had widened, that the cost of liabilities was not coming down even in what was supposed to be a lean period, not adequately anyway,” Neelkanth Mishra, Executive Director at the World Bank, told CNBC-TV18 on September 3.

title: Indian Banks now have to deploy ₹13 lakh crore of foreign inflows
